utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager, Kimberly Fleming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Defence counsel for Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The Chamber would like to greet everybody present here in the courtroom. We resume our proceedings. I would like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, and the accused. I would also like to greet all the staff in the courtroom, interpreters, representatives of the Registry, the usher, and everybody else. We are supposed to continue hearing the witness that we heard on Friday, but before that I would like to remind you of certain issues with regard to the schedule. We said we would not be sitting on Tuesday and that we would be sitting all day on Wednesday. There have been some changes in the meantime. Tomorrow we do have a courtroom at our disposal, so if the Prosecution is in the position to bring their witnesses tomorrow, and if the Defence does not object to that, tomorrow we can have a normal sitting at 14.15. Mr. Withopf, would you have any problems with continuing our proceedings tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we can actually reverse to the original schedule, which means that we will have one witness available for tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And now the Defence. I don't think that there will be any problems. You will be here tomorrow, I presume. Very well, then. Then we are going to proceed with the cross-examination of Mr. Totic. I would kindly ask the usher to bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Totic. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been in The Hague for almost five days. I hope that today's your last day. The cross-examination will continue. In order to do that, I'm turning towards the Defence, and the Defence, if they have new documents to tender, can you please tell us what is the source of the document and what is their purpose, if possible. So what is the purpose of these documents and their relevance. That will save us some time. And also, if you have those documents, can you please tender them one by one, not all of them at a time. So if possible, can you please tender your documents one at a time and can you provide us with all the relevant information about the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. On Friday, I showed a number of documents. And today I'm going to present to the witness four more documents, as I've already told you. And, Mr. President, since I have questions with regard to the already identified documents, I would like to ask questions about those first and then I will move on. And before I begin, I would like to apologise to the Trial Chamber. The document that I showed to the witness and that the witness recognised as the document issued by Commander Tihomir Blaskic, marked as DH45 ID due to technical error, when it was being copied, the three lines are missing from the first page. Over the weekend, the Defence has come across the complete order issued by Colonel Blaskic; and therefore, I would like for the document DH45 ID be presented to the witness first, and I would like the witness to identify this document as being the same, because this new document contains the entire item 4. We have provided the Chamber with the entire translation of the order, and over the weekend we have also come across with the French translation of this order and we would like to submit the French translation of this order and we would like it to be given a number for identification. So can the witness please be given the document DH45 ID, and at the same time could the usher give the Croatian version of the document which does not contain this technical error; i.e., where the item 4 is complete. Again, for the transcript, I would like to say that the identified document in English contains the entire item 4. At the same time, I would kindly ask the usher to give to the registrar the French translation of this order so that this translation could be given a number for identification. Could the Croatian version be given to the witness so he may compare this new version with the text that he was given on Friday and that he recognised already as an order issued by Colonel Blaskic. The error can be seen in the Croatian version, item 4. In the document that we presented to the witness on Friday, the words after the words "after the sector" are missing. The last three lines were lost in photocopying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Totic, did you understand what the problem is about? Last week the Defence has given you an order signed by Colonel Blaskic. This text contains several items; however, in the B/C/S version several lines are missing from item 4. The Defence realised that over the weekend. They realised that three lines are missing. That's why you are now being given a new copy of the same copy and this new copy contains the lines that were missing from the previous document. Mrs. Residovic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Totic, do you recognise the order that you were given by Colonel Blaskic on 16 January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I remember this order. There was indeed such an order. I cannot tell you that this is the order, but it seems to me that item 4 is something that was contained in the order. We're talking only about item 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since the witness realises that there was a technical error and that the three lines are an integral part of item 4, I would kindly ask for the document that was previously identified to be replaced by the document that has just been recognised by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Mr. Registrar, the new document that we have now received in B/C/S will be Exhibit DH45. In addition to that, the Defence counsel has given us the same document in French, and this document will be given number DH45/F. Can you please confirm what I've just said, Mr. Registrar. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that. I will take out the old version from the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These documents have been marked for identification, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, on Friday, I showed you some documents. Your order, number 288/92 of the 24th of October, 1992, which was marked for identification DH43 ID. I have shown you both versions, the B/C/S and the English. I have also shown you an order by the police administration dated 14 January 1993 signed by Valentin Coric and which was marked for identification DH47 ID. I also showed you an order of the Main Staff of the HVO, number 0166/93, dated 15 January 1993, signed by Milivoje Petkovic, which was given identification number DH2; and finally, an order of the Operative Zone Central Bosnia, that we have just sign; and finally, I showed you an order of the command of the Jure Francetic Brigade that you yourself signed, and that was marked for identification DH40 ID.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to give the order DH45 to the witness. This order was signed by Tihomir Blaskic. And also, DH46, an order signed by the witness. So can the usher please give these two orders to the witness so that I could ask him some questions about these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, is it correct that the order you issued on the 16th of January, 1993 was issued pursuant to the order of the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This order contained orders for all the HVO brigades and special orders for certain brigades and the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that I got it. I don't know whether the others got it. I suppose that all the addressees did receive it. I know that I received it. I don't know about the other addressees, whether they received it or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can tell who the addressees are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the order itself, you also see that it contains an order on raising the level of combat readiness to the highest level.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In its item 2, the order required several things from all the units: Firstly, under item 2 - can you please look at the lines - to have only two shifts on the front line and the rest of the troops to be in full combat readiness for interventions against Muslims. All the Muslims that do not obey commands should be disarmed and isolated. The troops from your brigade and the Nikola Subic Zrinski Brigade from Busovaca were ordered to organise reconnaissance in the area of the operation zone. Then the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade was also given orders. And under item 5, the 4th Battalion of the military police was given the task to control traffic and to stop all the transport of Muslims with arms, to seize the arms and put them at the disposal of the HVO. Does this order indeed contain all the things that I've just read out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were fully aware of the totality of the order and of the fact that the deadline for its execution was the 18th of January; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to this order, you knew that there was an order by the Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on the order of the commander of the operation zone, I could tell that he had received an order by the Main Staff of the HVO; however, I didn't see this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, can you please look at your order, which was marked for identification DH46 ID. Is it correct that in your order you also requested units to raise the level of combat readiness to the highest levels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also issued an order to the effect that all the Muslims who did not obey orders should be disarmed and isolated and that you should be informed about that urgently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did write that. But I would like to explain. In my brigade, I had soldiers, Muslims, Bosniaks; however, none of them were disarmed after this order. However, in the course of February and March 1993, a soldier, whose name is Dzemal Mahabasic in the town of Zenica threw a grenade and injured a child and a woman. He was drunk at the time. I gave him a prison sentence for 30 days, and after my exchange, I happened to go there because there was a depot there and went to control. I saw him there and asked him what he was doing there, and he told me that he was a guard. I was astonished. I was -- allow me, please. Allow me. After that, in 1994, this same soldier raped or attempted to rape somebody and then killed somebody. So he was already under sanctions. I did issue this order, but nobody was disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But we're still talking about January. So if there are any other questions we want to put to you, I'd be grateful for detailed information about such questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown a map, the map that he himself has marked, marked for identification DH44 ID. Could the witness hold on to his own order. Could you leave the order that the witness issued on the 16th of January with the witness, because the questions relate to his order and the map. DH46 ID and DH44 ID, could these two documents be shown to the witness. Could you put the map on the ELMO so that we can all see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Under item 3 of your order dated the 16th of January, would it be correct to say that you ordered the organisation and monitoring of all Muslim forces' movement? And could you please point out the following areas on the ELMO: The Brdo-Cajdras-Vjetrenice access; Brdo-Cajdras-Stranjani-Ovnak; Strajani-Ovnak-Radakovo-Lasva-Kaonik; Gradisce-Topola-Kozarci-Lokvine-Lupac and Gornja Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, didn't you ask me -- you didn't ask me to mark Gradisce last time. It hasn't been marked here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't seen it on the map, but if you know where it is located, you can mark that site.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can mark it with the following number: For the sake of the transcript, number 15 marks the location of Gradisce, according to the witness. Is it correct to say that under item 4 of that order you said that if there was an organised -- if there was organised movement of the Muslim forces all steps should be taken to stop them and all means should be used to stop them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that in addition to the orders given to the military police, whose task it was to intercept, disarm, and confiscate all the weapons and equipment of BH army members, these orders practically enabled you to surround the forces of the BH army in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that is correct. But the BH army forces at the time publicly said that they would use force to join up with the forces in Uskoplje. I didn't order anything else. All I order was that the BH army forces shouldn't pass through Croatian settlements. That is all I ordered.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those Croatian orders -- those Croatian settlements are settlements in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the BH army is the legitimate force there or was the legitimate force there. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the HVO was the legitimate force there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The deadline to carry out this order was the 18th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your order, in fact, amounted to implementing the order of the Main Staff of the 15th of January, according to which the forces of the operative zone of Central Bosnia should have all the directions in Central Bosnia blocked off, and it also meant executing the order of the operative zone. It was provided to you, this order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the execution of the commander of the operative zone, and I was under him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since the map represents a number of places and the witness himself has marked a number of places on the map and these places are the sites where the crimes alleged in the indictment were committed; and in addition, this map and the orders mentioned are elements which are essential to established command responsibility, especially the responsibility of commanders of a very high rank, it has to do with the question of taking measures and preventing crimes. This requires the establishment of a number of elements. It also requires establishing the situation with regard to combat operations in their area. So in my opinion, it is quite justified to ask that all identified documents be admitted into evidence as evidence for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I let Mr. Withopf take the floor, I have a few matters I would like to clarify. The order issued by Colonel Blaskic was written at 11.40. Apparently this order was forwarded to you by a messenger or courier. The order that you obtained was at 17.45, the order you obtained on the same day. So the order from Colonel Blaskic, you had it before 17.45.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we wouldn't receive the mail via courier. It was through packet communications. So this was immediately processed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The person who drafted the order, it wasn't you yourself. It must have been someone else who was within your headquarters and it was certainly a lawyer, because it's a fairly precise document. You had to sign it. Can you confirm that you drafted it or that someone else drafted it and that you only signed it? What could you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when this order was issued, in addition to my regular duties I was performing duties of the commander of Sector 2 for the Defence of Travnik. It was the Lasva-Kamenjas-Vradinac [phoen] access. And that's where you link up with the Ante Starcevic Brigade in Bugojno. The chief of the operations organ prepared this order, the chief of the operations organ in the brigade. He wasn't a lawyer. All orders are drafted in the operations and training organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When we compare your order and the one issued by your superior, there is an essential difference which appeared in paragraph 4 of your order. You say that you are ordering that all movement of Muslim forces be stopped, and in your superior's order, in the order issued by your superior, it says that all the Muslims who fail to obey orders should be disarmed, but the Muslims who are within HVO formations; whereas, your order goes far beyond what your superior's order states, because there it says that all the Muslim forces should be disarmed. How can you explain the fact that your order goes beyond what was ordered by your superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this order doesn't go beyond what was ordered by my superior, because under item 4 of my order it says: "In the case of an organised movement of Muslim forces, use all means at your disposal to stop them." So it mean that is the access that have been marked, the roads in that area were obstructed. The purpose of that order was to prevent an escalation of the conflict, to prevent Muslim forces from passing through Croatian settlements which would have frightened the people and the situation would have got out of hand. From September -- in fact, even from August, the tension was increasing and the conflict on the 20th of June in Novi Travnik and Vitez and in Uskoplje; that is to say, in Prozor, on the 23rd and the 24th. We were at the edge of a conflict at that time. The purpose was just to prevent any further escalation. I wouldn't have been in a position to carry out to disarming of the Muslim forces, because they were -- they were seven times as strong as we were in Zenica. I could only try to prevent an organised movement, and there was nothing else I could do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My last question: In your order in B/C/S - and it wasn't translated into English - your order is 80 - 699. We can't see the number very well. This order seems to be one of a series of orders. How do you explain that this order doesn't mention above your title of commander of the Jure Francetic Brigade the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is what is mentioned in your superior's order? Because your superior's order contains the mention "The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Defence Council," et cetera. And oddly enough, you don't refer to any of these items. It comes directly from the command. All the orders that you sign, did they always fail to mention the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna? What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this order was drafted in accordance with instructions for issues combat orders. So when I carried out orders -- when I issued orders, it wasn't necessary for me to mention this. I only had to mark the number, state the level of confidentiality, and say when it was issued and what the command post was. And it was taken for granted that this is where the orders from superiors would come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Withopf, you wanted to comment on the Defence's question? Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. The Prosecution objects against tendering the map and the entirety of the documents which have been marked for identification into evidence, and we object for a number of reasons. The October 1992 order, we cannot see any relevance, if at all; that's at least our interpretation. The 16th January 1993 orders of Blaskic and the order of the witness, if at all, they can be related to the crime committed in Dusina, which was committed on the 26th of January, 1993. The Prosecution made it clear in its pre-trial brief that in relation to Dusina, since it's the first crime, the first in chronological order, the accused Hadzihasanovic can only be held criminally liable for failure to punish and not for failure to prevent. The micro-military situation in the area of Zenica -- and if one has a look at the map which has been marked for identification, it's actually the wider area of Zenica and only, if at all, only a very narrowed-down area is in any respect related to Dusina -- this situation can't play any role in respect to failure to punish. The map, the map itself, my learned colleague made the witness identify 14 locations. Out of the 14 locations, there are only three locations which appear - which appear - to some extent related to the crimes which are incorporated in the indictment. Again, the Prosecution fails to see the relevance of the map. I also want to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber that the witness last Friday, in respect to the Blaskic order, which is marked with the number 45 for identification, actually challenged the signature of Mr. Blaskic. Again, the Prosecution fails to understand and cannot see the relevance of the entirety of all documents which Defence tries to tender into evidence. We object against tendering such documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have taken note Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of your objection and we will rule on it, naturally. The Prosecution [as interpreted] May proceed with its questions relating to the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I would like to just say one thing about the relevance of the documents. The map clearly shows the areas that have been referred to in the indictment and to Ovnak, Zenica, Dusina, Lasva, which are also places contained in the indictment, and therefore the map itself is relevant. As far as other documents are concerned, especially the one that my learned colleague from the Prosecution has referred to dated the 24th of October, with regard to the theory and the jurisprudence of this Trial Chamber, the modus operandi is one of the key issues that has to be examined when determining command responsibility. And in the order that this witness issued on the 24th of October, tasks are mentioned which indicate that there are hostilities in relation to the army: Prevent the BH army forces from passing through certain areas, Zenica -- Dusina, Zenica, Ovnak. And then it says about taking up positions from October -- the HVO had surrounded the majority of the forces of the BH army in Zenica. And this has to do with all the activities of the commander and will enable one to assess his capability of observing the entire situation and finding out about certain events and taking certain measures. Since the decisions that this Tribunal has taken confirm that this is a relevant matter, I stand by my suggestion, and the Trial Chamber naturally will rule on the matter. We will respect its decisions. I will now carry on with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, since you said that you are familiar with the entire order issued by Colonel Blaskic and you are also familiar with the part that related to the military police --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document 0243077593 dated 21 of September [as interpreted], signed by Pasko Ljubicic. We have a sufficient number of copies for the Trial Chamber, for the Prosecution, and for the others present in the courtroom. Can we have a number for identification of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you give us an identification number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be DH48, marked for identification for the B/C/S version; and DH48/E, marked for identification for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, this document, issued by the military police, does it also arise from the same order, number 011184/93, which was issued by Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this document is referred to herein.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the transcript, there is an error. I said that the date of this document is 20 January, and in line 2, on page 17, the date that is indicated is 25 September, so I would like the date to be corrected for the transcript. I believe that now the document has been fully identified.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can the witness be shown the two following documents that this witness has assigned on the following dates: 30 January 1993 and 2 February 1993. At the same time, could both documents be given identification numbers. I'm giving the witness two documents at the same time because I'm going to be asking one or two questions that refer to both documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, did you issue the order on the 30th January 1993 titled "Sending unit to Busovaca"? And in this order, under item 1, you order as follows: "The anti-sabotage unit of the Jure Francetic Brigade should be sent to Busovaca in order to help the Zrinski Brigade," and the aim was to carry out combat operations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is true that I issued this order. I don't know which unit it was. This is not signed. I know that I sent some 40 or 50 troops for temporary assistance and only with defensive goals, not any other goal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have an identification number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Totic, can you please explain -- this order bears your name and "SR," about in English and in B/C/S. What does "SR" stand for? We don't see your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means "in one's own hand." I can't confirm exactly whether this order exists or not. I know that I did issue such orders but not in this form. Whatever was sent through confidential means could not be signed. However, the archived copies are signed. I don't know whether an order did exist in this form or not. I can't tell you. I remember that I did issue orders to that effect; whether they were in this form, I can't remember at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Totic, it is not disputable that you sent some 50 of your troops to Busovaca to assist the Zrinski Brigade in order to carry out combat operations against the BH army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is correct. On the 23rd to 25th, about 8 and 5 thousand troops [as interpreted] of the BH army carried out an attack from all directions on Busovaca. And the Busovaca Brigade had only 1700 troops to defend itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have an identification number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Mr. Registrar, can we please have a number for identification, the document that was sent on the 30th January by Mr. Totic. Can we please have two numbers, one for the English version and one for the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number for the B/C/S version will be DH49, marked for identification; and the number for the English version will be DH49/E, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to this document, Mr. Totic, can you tell me whether you recognise the stamp on the document. The stamp contains the date and the time when your order was dispatched.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not a stamp, Your Honours. This is just a seal which existed in the communications department. I do not know this signature and I can't say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please look at your combat order, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. We have a problem here. The order was sent on the 30th January, and the time indicated here is 1.15. This is on the left-hand side. And the seal that we can see below, showing the words "HVO Vitez," one would say that this document was received on the 30th January at 15.40 hours. So we seem to be having some problems here. One would say, -- as a matter of fact, no, I've been confused. Yes, the document was dispatched at 13.10 and received at 15.40. That's okay. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, in front of you you have your order 04/93, which was sent to the commanders of the 1st and 2nd Battalions under the number 184/93, on the 2nd of February, 1993. Did you issue this order or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This order orders the commanders of your battalions to send to the Kuber [Realtime transcript read in error: Bugara] Sector where there are some 50 or 60 troops, and that they should be linked up with the HVO Vitez troops.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. In the Kubura Sector [as interpreted], I had one platoon from 1992 onwards; and here I am ordering them to link up with the adjacent unit. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, you participate as a brigade from Zenica in the activities of the HVO troops in Busovaca and Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we did not encircle the BH army troops. We just prevented any movements of the BH army and their transfer to Uskoplje and Prozor, and further on towards Vitez and the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that we have an error calami in the transcript, page 20, line 20. It says: "In the Kubura Sector." It should be the Kuber Sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. So it is Kuber sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the reasons I have stated a little while ago, these orders permanently - up to the events in Dusina and even after that - determine the activities of the commander of the 3rd Corps. I believe that these are relevant documents and orders, and for that reason I would like to tender these two orders, as well as the order of the military police, which was an integral part of the attacks organised against the BH army, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Mr. Withopf, I would like to summarise the objections put forth by the Defence. The Defence believes that all these documents are relevant because according to the Defence counsel they indicate that the HVO, and primarily the Jure Francetic Brigade, started encircling the BH army troops and encircled them completely. And since this constitutes a modus operandi, and for that reason, these documents should be tendered into evidence, and this is the essence of their arguments. Mr. Withopf, you've heard the arguments put forth by the Defence regard to the relevance of these documents. What can you tell us? What are your observations with this regard? I have the impression that you wanted to say something. You were on your feet. Have you understood the position of the Defence? The Defence tells us that all these documents should be tendered because they establish that the orders were issued and the witness was in a very high military position, and that all these orders were aimed at encircling the BH army. Since these documents prove that there was an intent to encircle the BH army troops, these documents should therefore be admitted into evidence. What can you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand you are summarising the Defence position, and I have my doubts whether the witness actually confirmed the Defence position, but that's a different issue. The Prosecution objects, again, to tendering these documents into evidence, again for a number of reasons: First of all, the Prosecution is quite surprised for the reason that there is no dispute that from January 1993 onwards until March 1994 there was a conflict between the HVO and the ABiH in the area of Central Bosnia, including the areas which have been addressed and which are covered by the documents Defence try to tender into evidence. I refer to paragraph 26 of the Third Amended Indictment. In relation to the documents themselves, the document which has been marked for identification under DH48 ID, the witness has only confirmed what is written in the document. He has not even been asked whether he ever has seen this order. The witness for that reason hasn't said anything and hasn't testified to any extent in relation to this document. For that only reason, it should not be tendered into evidence. In relation to the document which is marked for identification under DH49 ID, the witness actually challenged the authenticity of the document. And in relation to the witness -- to the document which is marked for identification under DH50 ID, there is reference made to a location, which is obviously a village with the name of Kuber. This village is not marked in the map which has been given to the witness to identify certain locations. Again, the Prosecution fails to understand and does not understand the relevance of all such documents. Defence must, in order to get these documents be tendered into evidence, follow certain steps. And if they want to show - and that's the interpretation of the Defence line - that the accused Hadzihasanovic at the relevant point in time was too busy dealing with military matters and, in brackets, the military matters addressed in this order appear to be quite minor ones, if the Defence position is that the accused Hadzihasanovic was too busy, then they must show in far more detail why such movements of troops had an impact on the ability of the accused Hadzihasanovic to punish the crime in Dusina. For these varieties of reasons, the Prosecution objects against tendering these documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just a few words, if I may. The Third Amended indictment, under 39, clearly indicates that the forces of the 3rd Corps - that is, the last sentence - "The killings that were carried out after the attack on towns and villages were by the troops of the 3rd Corps of Bosnia and Herzegovina." So in -- under item 39 and the item quoted by himself shows clearly what the position of the BH army was. All the orders that have been presented speak to the contrary. Secondly, I would like to thank my learned friend, and I believe that as a future Defence counsel he will be in a good position to analyse the importance of documents tendered by the Defence. The documents speak for themselves, and the Defence, when the time comes, if they are tendered into evidence, will provide their analysis and significance from the point of view of the defence of General Hadzihasanovic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I'd like to point out that the witness should indicate the Kuber area on the map, because we don't know where it is. So the witness has to be shown the map again so that he can mark the site. He has the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness has marked "Kuber" on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is no village called Kuber. It's an elevation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the witness has already marked it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I carry on, could the last document be marked for identification. I would like to repeat the Defence's suggestion, that these documents should be admitted into evidence, the document dated the 2nd of February signed by the witness. Could this document be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the document dated the 2nd of February and signed by the witness - and we can see the stamp of the republic and his signature, and we see that the order mentions the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina - there is also a reference made to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. We need a number for the B/C/S and English version, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the number for the B/C/S version will be DH50, marked for identification; and the number for the English version will be DH50/E, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, we'll now go back to some other issues that you have already spoken about to my learned colleagues from the Prosecution. You said that in 1991 in December you finished a one-year training course in the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a high military school, and it lasts two years.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After having completed that course, you received a certain rank, the rank of second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then you were assigned to duties at the Bihac airport.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was the engineers company in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that school, you didn't continue with your education in the army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But I had previously worked for ten years as a non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I haven't understood you correctly. So that was the last school that you completed in the course of your military clear; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You never graduated from the military academy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The rank of a non-commissioned officer which you received at the time was in fact a rank which was the first officer's rank in the former JNA -- or, rather, it was the lowest rank of an officer in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's the first rank that an officer can obtain.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, your experience in the JNA was experience you had gained as a non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your specialty is engineering; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the Bihac -- at the Bihac airport, you were assigned as a platoon commander, and you were in charge of about 100 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the commander of the 2nd Engineer's Company, and there were about 120, 150 men in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your task was to provide engineering security for the airport with that company of 100 or 150 men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't to provide engineering support -- it was to provide engineering support in the zone of responsibility of the airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You never finished the staff school for officer; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Up until the war, apart from being involved in engineering, you weren't involved in strategy or in sabotage operations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. But if you take into consideration the engineers and its composition, its composition included certain specialties, for example explosives, booby-traps, and reconnaissance units. So this was included in the training.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had the rank of a brigadier. That's not a general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it isn't. That's the rank of a brigadier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You obtained that rank thanks to the fact that you participated in the war and you performed certain military and political duties in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only military duties. I didn't perform political duties of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So your rank or, rather, your profession didn't correspond to your military education, because you couldn't have obtained that rank in the former JNA, given the schooling that you had completed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in fact 95 per cent of officers in the Federation army in fact have no qualifications. In order to be a general, you require certain qualifications. You need a Ph.D. sometimes. We have a lot of generals, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In response to a question from the Prosecution and also in response to my questions, you said that the Municipal Staff of the HVO in Zenica became the brigade staff in a certain period when it was being reorganised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The command of the brigade, from the 4th to the 18th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In December, a solemn oath was taken in the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This oath was attended by -- taking this oath was attended by Dario Kordic, Colonel Blaskic, and other prominent people, for example, army representatives.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers who were taking their oaths were also addressed by Dario Kordic. You addressed them, as the commander; as well as Tihomir Blaskic, as the commander of the operative zone. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown an extract from the magazine called "Bojovnik," combatant, dated December 1992, and it relates to the addresses of the persons mentioned. In the course of our investigations, we found the texts in the Kordic case. It was also shown to the witness in that case. And in accordance with the instructions issued by the Trial Chamber, the parts that we will be showing to the witness have been translated into French as well as into English.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, you know that "Bojovnik" was a magazine from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Zenica HVO; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that Mr. Dario Kordic, when addressing the soldiers, did so in Zenica? He addressed them in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know that he addressed the soldiers, but I really don't know what was said by the various people present at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'll remind you. According to the magazine that you've already been shown, Dario Kordic said, "It's a great pleasure for me to be present here today and in such numbers. I'm glad that we are on Croatian territory, on the unified territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The Croatian territory of Zenica was Croatian and still is Croatian and it will remain Croatian territory. This will be the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, regardless of whether people like this or not." Do you remember Dario Kordic saying these words at that ceremony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember what Dario Kordic said on that occasion, so that was his address. I can't confirm that those were his exact words, but the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, who is bothered by the existence of this community in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, did you too address your soldiers on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now referring to what it says beneath the words "the commander of the staff." Did you say: "We have taken the solemn oath within the brigade, whose name is Jure Francetic. All those who don't like this holy name, well, I would like to tell them that Jure Francetic, who was a Croatian knight, fought with the Serbs in the solemn war. In the Second World War, he protected the Croatian and Bosnian people and expelled the Chetniks from Romanija and the left bank of the Drina." As he has -- follows [as interpreted], "there is nothing that we want." Is that what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said something in effect to that. But all I did was refer to his military skills.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You - and that's my case too - you know from history, from what we learned about history. But I won't refer to what we know, I'll refer to a Croatian TV programme. In the 313th series of "Latinica" by Denis Latin dated the 16th of February, 2004, it says that Francetic Jure was born in 912 [as interpreted], and that in the independent state of Croatia he was assigned as the commander of Eastern Croatia with its basis in Sarajevo. And towards the end of 1941 he created -- founded the Black League. And on the Internet there are numerous articles which refer to the Black League and say it was founded -- and it imitated the SS troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object against such a line of questioning. The Prosecution can't see the relevance of the historical explanation and irrespective whether it's true or not, of the historical explanation of the name that has given the brigade the witness commanded at the time. Defence may please explain the relevance of such line of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. With regard to the relevance, could you tell the Trial Chamber what the relevance is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the reason for making these references is that the witness said that we were dealing with a Croatian knight. And in the course of its cross-examination, counsel can try to discredit the witness by asking him questions. Since his brigade had been called after a well-known person in charge of the Black League in Bosnia and Herzegovina, responsible for many crimes committed against the Serbian and Jewish and anti-fascist peoples, including the Croatian and Muslim ones, I think that it is important for this reason to admit this fact as evidence that could discredit the witness. And secondly, we would like to tender this document into evidence. In 1992, this man, together with Ante Pavelic, was received by Adolf Hitler. And in the Second World War, his crimes were very well known. And for these reasons, in order to discredit this witness, we suggest that this be admitted into evidence. And the words of Dario Kordic, as well as the words of this witness, quite clearly indicate the position that the BH army was in when all this was said in the centre of Zenica. And according to what the witness himself said at the time, the centre was over 80 per cent Bosniak. And finally, these are the words of a man who has spoken about a man who has denied Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state and denied the existence of the Bosniak people as a people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I please briefly respond? Mr. President, Your Honours, this goes far, far beyond the scope of any relevance, and Defence may please ask the witness whether he has chosen the name of the brigade he commanded at the time. And if Defence wishes to follow up this line and if the Chamber is inclined to grant leave for Defence to follow up this line of questioning, any evidential value can only be based on the independent assessment of an expert, an historical expert, who can judge on these issues. The Defence is trying to introduce in this trial historical facts, and nobody knows whether they are true or not. At least for the time being, without having laid any basis for this line of questioning - and the basis can only be laid by an expert on the very same issues - Defence should not be allowed to continue with this line of questioning. The Prosecution objects, and the Prosecution strongly suggests that the Trial Chamber rules on this issue prior to giving Defence a chance to continue this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President -- Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We are first going to have a break, and we will discuss this issue and render our decision. Let me sum up. Your question to the witness was whether he knows who Francetic actually was and that was the main objective of your question. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The witness mentioned him, and then I asked the witness whether that person was what I said he was, and the witness reacted. Your Honours, we are tendering this into evidence only to go for the credibility of the witness, and this will actually complete my cross-examination. And before that, can we please have a number for the identification of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We are going to give you our answer after the break. It is twenty to 4.00. We shall resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We continue our hearing. As far as the admission of documents is concerned - and we are talking about the article from "Bojovnik." After having deliberated, Trial Chamber comes to the following decision: It will not be admitted into evidence in view of the fact that the document does not go as to the credibility of the witness. The Trial Chamber would like to stress the following fact: The credibility of a witness cannot challenged based on historical facts which go back in time and precede the period during which the events in the indictment took place. For that reason, this document is not going to be admitted into evidence. The Trial Chamber also would like to underline the following: Regarding the questions that have been put to the witness, the Trial Chamber does not try the HVO or members of the HVO. So the Defence may put questions to a former member of the HVO under the following conditions: These questions have to concern only the relevant military aspect and the questions that concern the fact that the witness was an eyewitness to. In conclusion, I would like to repeat: This document is not going to be admitted into evidence. As far as the other documents are concerned, they have been marked for identification, and the Trial Chamber will make a decision about these documents subsequently, in keeping with what we are going to hear from other witnesses or based on new evidence. I am now turning to the other Defence counsel. Does the Defence counsel for Mr. Kubura want to cross-examine Mr. Totic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we do have some questions for Mr. Totic. Our cross-examination will concern only what the witness said on his examination-in-chief last Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Totic, during your stay in Zenica, in the course of 1992 and 1993, while you were a member of the Main Staff of the HVO and a brigade commander, you did not have an opportunity to meet -- officially meet Mr. Kubura; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not know Brigadier Kubura in 1992 or 1993. Maybe I may have met him in 1997 if he was a member of the federation army. I may have seen him as a meeting. But I can't be sure even of that. I've never spoken to him. I have never officially met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief, on two occasions, on Friday you said before this Trial Chamber that you do not have enough information about the 7th Muslim Brigade in 1992 and 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is correct. It is correct that I stated that. We did not have much information. I only know that it originated from the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Zenica up to April 1993, you were never in the staff of the 7th Muslim Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I was never there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You did not have an opportunity to meet with any other officer of the 7th Muslim Brigade during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never met any of them. All I know, according to the information that I had, is that Mr. Kubura was its commander. However, according to some rumours, there were other more influential people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You also said on Friday that you had testified in the Kordic case as a Defence witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about some problems that arose from the insignia worn by the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what context was that part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You were presented an order that you issued on the 9th of February, 1993, when pursuant to this order all the insignia that did not indicate the affiliation with the HVO should be removed from the uniforms of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is true; I issued that order pursuant to the order of the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and the aim was for all the soldiers of the HVO to be forced to remove insignia from their uniform that would point to anything that was not in keeping with the times and the period that we lived in -- old insignia that would be -- that could be associated with the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you gave an explanation to the Trial Chamber, and you said that it was very popular at the time, that it was a fad to wear all sorts of insignia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that this was also popular with the members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you described the insignia of the 7th Muslim Brigade and you recognised it in the exhibit presented to you by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The insignia bear the name of the 7th Muslim Brigade, and there's also an Arabic inscription; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind your professional experience working in the army for over 30 years, from the year 1974 when you started your military education, and then you continued working with the troops, and then in the war you were a brigade commander, can you agree with me that in order for you to recognise whether a soldier belongs to a unit such a soldier has to wear all the proper insignia? That is the only way you can be sure of the fact that a soldier belongs to a certain unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in order to be absolutely sure, the soldier has to wear all the legal insignia. The 7th Muslim Brigade - and it's insignia that was recognised here - based on that, one could recognise the unit. It is to be assumed that the Muslim -- that the 7th Brigade was part of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can you agree with me if there are no proper identified -- insignia to identify a soldier and his affiliation, you cannot be sure of the soldier's affiliation to any unit? Can you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, more or less I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just a short question for clarification of a military matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have testified that you had a Department for Intelligence, an intelligence unit within your brigade. Can you please tell us whether within your zone there was an Intelligence Department or section. Did you have such a thing at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, every brigade has a Department for Intelligence, and this department is headed by the intelligence officer who is the head of that department. And all the information that I received came from the Chief of Intelligence, who was a member of the brigade. As for the first units of Muslim forces, I learned about them from the Chief of Intelligence. The first time I ever saw these insignia was in July or August 1992 in the Pasinac Sector. The HVO, the 2nd Battalion, had its camp there. Immediately after that, some 15 or 20 days later, a Territorial Defence unit was positioned some 6 or 7 hundred metres as the crow flies from that camp. At that time, from a vehicle I saw people with the insignia of Muslim brigades. That was the first time I saw them. They were mixed with the people who were members of the Territorial Defence. The second time I saw people wearing the insignia of Muslim forces was when I commanded the Sector 2 for the defence of Travnik. In one part, in front of the front line there were two Muslim villages, Bijelo Buce and Pulac. And every evening I would open the front line in order to let the BH army troops through those places. They didn't want to leave those villages, or they were between the two front lines, between the Serb forces on the one hand, and the HVO on the other hand. In November 1992, for the second time I saw the insignia of Muslim forces on people wearing them. And later on, in 1993, this was a common sight. So we knew that in every village there was at least one platoon of Muslim forces. There are also some very bad experiences with these Muslim forces. For example, in the place where I was born, the BH army forces, if they captured somebody, they would hide those Croats in their houses and they were afraid that somebody from the Muslim forces would hear about them, because in that case they would have to execute them. There are Croat people who survived owing to the solidarity of the local Muslim population, who prevented their execution. They didn't want to hand them over to members of the Muslim forces. And that's how these people survived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You also indicated that you had an officer for intelligence in your brigade. Tell us, did this department intercept telephone conversations of other units, or was it just intelligence based on surveillance, monitoring, and conveying things that they happened to hear by chance? Did this unit have any kind of logistics that would enable it to intercept telephone conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the intelligence unit in the brigades was not technically equipped for interception. It was done at higher levels, at the operative zone level and higher levels. Within the brigade, the intelligence department had a platoon that consisted of some 50 to 70 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am giving the floor to Mr. Withopf for re-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. The re-examination will actually be quite brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Totic, asked on Friday by my learned colleague on the Defence side at the very beginning of the cross-examination, you said - and that's page 43, lines 2 to 14 of the Friday's transcript - you said that "At the beginning of the war, between 35.000 and 40.000 Muslims from Eastern Bosnia and Krajina arrived in Zenica." And in answering the respective question of my learned colleague whether these people were mainly Muslims or Bosniaks, you confirmed that "About 90 per cent of the refugees were Muslims or Bosniaks." To your knowledge, within the 35.000 to 40.000 Muslims arriving from Eastern Bosnia and the Krajina, were there also men of military age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there were able-bodied men among those people, and from the territory of Western Bosnia only, after the fall of Jajce, towards the end of October 1992. With these people, the 305th Mountain Brigade came together with the refugees, which was later on incorporated in the 3rd Corps. Their command post was in Biljesovo, near Zenica. Also, in 1991, near the territory of Central Bosnia, the 17th Krajina Brigade was deployed, which consisted mostly of people from Bosanska Krajina, of people who were able-bodied. Some of them had even completed military training and were armed in the Borongaj barracks in Zagreb in Croatia, and they came in Travnik. So these were people who were not locals but they operated and played a significant role in the operations of the 3rd Corps in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You basically answered the question, Mr. Totic. Within the 35.000 to 40.000 refugees, to your knowledge, did a significant number - and if you know in rough terms of the number, can you please tell the Trial Chamber how many of such refugees became members of the ABiH 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot say that for a fact, but at least two brigades were formed of these people, the 305th and the 17th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And at the time and in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, of how many troops was a brigade comprised of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended on the type of the brigade, but it ranged from 1900 to 3500 men, and most often 2.700. And that was at least what the situation was in the organisation of the HVO brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In answering a question put to you by my learned colleague today, you were saying that the ABiH was seven times as strong as the HVO. Does this also apply for the area of the 3rd Corps in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the ratio was 1 to 8 for the zone of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In favour of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In favour of the BiH army, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Totic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This concludes the re-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Totic, you have spent five days in The Hague. You have testified for two entire days. You have answered the Prosecutor's questions, then the Defence questions. You have also answered questions put to you by the Trial Chamber. Thank you for coming to testify. Your testimony is going to help us arrive at the truth about these events. Thank you very much. We wish you a happy journey back home. I am kindly asking the usher to take you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf -- before I give you the floor, Mr. Bourgon would like the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. With your permission, I would like to address the Trial Chamber with regard to the decision on the admissibility of certain documents that have been used in the cross-examination of Mr. Totic. Mr. President, the objection of my observation is for the clarification of the procedure with regard to the admission of documents, especially those documents that may be considered admissible. I would like to start with your decision rendered on the 17th of February, and I would like to present the views of the Defence. The way we understood your decision, the Trial Chamber said that it is up to both sides to determine in advance the relevance of any document and then that the relevance is based on the facts and information that may be presented by a witness, that the relevance can also be based on military, political, and historical facts from the period. You also said that the Trial Chamber wants to adopt a general interpretation of the admissibility of documents and that the only exception is when the authenticity of a document is contested. And if such a document is contested, then the side who tenders a document for admission has to confirm its authenticity. When rendering this document, the Trial Chamber has also mentioned the context which is different for an expert witness and for a factual witness. And you said that for an expert witness that the side has to submit the written document in advance and also the Trial Chamber has asked both sides to present a list of the contested documents and also list the documents that will be used during cross-examination. The position of the Defence today is as follows: We believe that it is very important for the Trial Chamber to, at the moment when we ask for a document to be admitted, that at that moment the Trial Chamber should render its decision on the admissibility of a document. If the decision rendered by the Trial Chamber on the 17th February is still valid, then we believe that if the document is relevant the Trial Chamber has to state whether a document is admissible or not. In the case that we are facing today - and I am referring to the decision that you rendered earlier on today, when you said that a decision on the admissibility of certain documents will be made subsequently - amongst those documents was a geographic map on which the witness marked certain places and numbered them. In addition to that, the witness pointed to certain regions on the map, and the map itself is the map of the general area of Zenica, that is, villages and hamlets around Zenica. During the cross-examination led by my colleague, we heard answers that spoke of the relevance of this document with regard to the orders issued by today's witness. He explained what the purpose of the orders was and where they stemmed from and what was the military context within which those orders were issued in the period from January 1993 onwards. Your Honours, we believe that all the documents that originate from the Main Staff of the HVO -- documents that were issued by General Petkovic, who was General Blaskic's superior, then documents issued by General Blaskic and sent to Brigadier Tokic [phoen], followed by the orders issued by Totic, several of them -- those orders were then conveyed to subordinate units. I'm talking about documents DH43. These are documents issued by the military police and orders giving certain, very precise tasks to the military police. I would like to emphasise the following: All these documents describe the context within which the parties acted, and this context, contrary to what has been stated by the Prosecutor, the purpose was not to prove that the accused was preoccupied with certain things in order to prevent crimes and punishing criminals. This was not the purpose. The main purpose was our wish to describe for the Trial Chamber the context within which the accused acted, within which he was forced to make decisions, the context in which the events happened. And he has been charged with certain things that happened at that time. Only if you're aware of the context you may judge whether he is guilty or not. He was on the ground. He commanded the corps. And you already know that he had a large number of troops under him. And that's why we believe it is very important for the Trial Chamber to be well informed about the context. This is our approach, and has been from the very beginning. We have never departed from that approach, from our pre-trial brief to this very day. And in that sense, we have asked the Trial Chamber to take into account some adjudicated facts. All this are elements which we consider that have to be taken into account by the Trial Chamber when rendering certain decisions. And in conclusion, Mr. President, I would like to address the issue of procedure that we have to adopt. One thing we have to be clear on. With your permission, I would like to tell you what exactly has been happening before the trial -- before this Tribunal. In the Tadic case in 1995 - this was the first trial that was ever conducted before this International Tribunal - at that time, the procedure for admitting documents into evidence was similar to the procedure in the Anglo-Saxon system, which means that documents were admitted through witnesses. Every time the witness had to recognise and confirm the authenticity of the document, and this dealt with the authenticity and the relevance of any document. The decision was rendered immediately as to whether such a document would be admitted or not, and if such a document was admitted, then the document was identified. However, the position of the Defence is that if a document is only marked for identification purposes, that means nothing. That only means that the document will be held by the registrar until the moment its lot is dealt with. In the meantime, the procedure has changed. In the later cases, in order to speed up the procedure, there have been some changes. For example, in the Simic case, all the documents were admitted into evidence during the pre-trial procedure, before the trial itself, and then the Trial Chamber decided that if none of the witnesses confirmed the existence of a certain document or if they didn't present further information on this document, then these documents were not considered to have any probative value. Another example: In the Blaskic case, towards the end of the procedure, the Trial Chamber allowed both sides to deliver and submit documents which were not tendered through witnesses, and then it was up to the Trial Chamber to determine the probative value. If you look at the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, you will see that there are very few rules on admission of exhibits into evidence. In any case, Rule 89 is the Rule of the uttermost significance. It says if a document is relevant it may be admitted, and it's up to the Trial Chamber to determine its probative value, and this can be done even without a witness . For example, we can draw a parallel here: The second-hand evidence. You are going to hear a witness who is going to be -- give you secondhand testimony. The rule of this Tribunal is to admit hearsay, despite the fact that the person who said something to the witness is not known. So even if we are dealing with hearsay, this is admitted as evidence. The Trial Chamber here admits hearsay evidence and considers it relevant. With all due respect, Your Honours, we ask from the Trial Chamber to explain the procedure to us. Is the Trial Chamber going to continue working in the following way, and that is documents will be tendered through witnesses, or the Trial Chamber is going to adopt a procedure which is going to be somewhat closer and somewhat more similar that was adopted in some other cases? The Defence is prepared to accept any decision rendered by the Trial Chamber, but we believe that we should be better informed of the position of the Trial Chamber and what the Trial Chamber believes needs to be done in respect of the admissibility of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Bourgon, for your comments. We've been aware of the problem from the very beginning. You have quite rightly said that the procedure before this Tribunal has differed. You mentioned the Tadic case, and the procedure followed in that case was very similar to the common-law procedure. One would tender a document into evidence through a witness. And you pointed out that in another case, the Simic case, all the documents had been tendered into evidence in the pre-trial stage. And then the third procedure adopted concerned the Blaskic case, in which documents were filed. These three manners of proceeding are naturally interesting and are not in question for the Trial Chamber. They are recognised by the Trial Chamber. It is for the parties to decide as to what the best way of presenting its argument would be and to see at what point in time they should tender a document into evidence. For the moment, we haven't obstructed your manner of proceeding. We have admitted almost all the documents. It seems that you are somewhat concerned about the documents that have been marked for identification, and a minute ago you mentioned a particular example; namely, the map.
