When we mark a document for identification, the Trial Chamber considers that this means that we will be rendering a decision. The document won't be on standby indefinitely. We will take a decision about giving certain documents exhibit numbers. But nevertheless, we need to be able to take a decision in the light of other factors, and it is at that stage that we go back to the motion that is still pending; that is to say, the admission into evidence of matters that have been dealt with by the cases. We are elaborating a decision, and this decision will state why we have decided to mark certain documents for identification, for the time being. All this will enable you to have a better view of the situation. And at the moment, I think there are between eight and ten documents that have been marked for identification. We will be rendering a decision, naturally. The fact that we have said that documents have been marked for identification doesn't mean that we will be forgetting about these documents. You have suggested that a decision should be rendered immediately, as far as the relevance of documents are concerned. And we might then reject documents which could subsequently be revealed as important, given that witnesses called say that the documents are important, they recognise them. So this would be detrimental to both parties if a document was rejected in this manner. So this is why we will consider the matter of rejecting a document, because when you reject a document this means that it can't be presented again, unless there are exceptional circumstances. So there might be borderline cases, cases in which a document might be rejected, but rejecting such a document might be detrimental to someone. So in such a case, we would prefer to mark a document for identification because a document that doesn't seem to be relevant might subsequently be seen to be quite relevant. So that is why we have eight or ten documents that have been marked for identification. You have suggested tendering documents into evidence as was done in the Blaskic case. The Trial Chamber doesn't see any difficulty there; but nevertheless, your list of documents still has to be provided to the Prosecution, to make sure that they have no objections to raise. Because the problem is that the Prosecution might not be in agreement with you. And the inverse case might happen; the Prosecution might want to tender a lot of documents into evidence and you might not be in agreement. So the parties, you may have admitted very few facts and a lot might be contested. So one party might arrive with a long list of documents and the other party might accept them as such. If you have discussions and you reach an agreement as to the documents you might have, the documents you might present - for example, rules on military tribunals in Bosnia and Herzegovina that have to do with the Constitution, the constitutional decision, et cetera - if there is no disagreement, naturally this will be to everyone's benefit. But you have both realised that you are not in agreement for the moment, so I don't see how you might establish a list which could be accepted by the opposing side. But you can always try to do this. It's not prohibited. If you are not able to do so, then the documents will be tendered into evidence as the witnesses appear. This is what was done in the Tadic case. This is a very common law procedure, and naturally we will accept such a procedure because it makes it possible to have adversarial proceedings that concern the documents. And this has been the case to date. The fear you have expressed is that the Trial Chamber, given the expert witnesses who appear, the observers who appear, and so on, in such cases we might have a lot of documents. If both parties manage to reach an agreement with regard to these documents, we will not waste time. And if that is the case, then you just have to indicate that on the list document 43 is being tendered into evidence by the Defence or by the Prosecution, and naturally we will immediately consult document 43. So we don't exclude anything. We will accept any type of procedure, providing that the procedure enables us to save time. But the Prosecution also has to inform me of their position with regard to the issues raised by the Defence and with regard to the possibilities we might have of saving time when dealing with documents, because in the days or weeks to come we will probably be faced with a lot of documents and we have to find a way of saving time. So perhaps Mr. Withopf will have something to say that might be in agreement with what the Defence has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. Since my learned friend from the Defence side addressed three issues - namely, the Totic-related documents, the broader issue of the military and political context, and the even broader issue of tendering documents in future - I wish to address these issues in the order just mentioned. In respect to the documents related to the witness Totic, I can be very brief. I reiterate what we said earlier on today and during the examination-in-chief -- during the cross-examination of the witness Totic. In respect to a number of documents, the witness did not even comment on the documents. He only confirmed what my learned colleague from the Defence said read out to him. In respect to any documents which could be of relevance or which in the opinion of Defence may be of relevance, in relation to the crime that was committed in Dusina, we emphasise that only the failure-to-punish aspect can be of relevance in that respect. In respect to the broader issue of what is the military, political, and if I'm not wrong, the Chamber even said the economical context of the crimes or in respect to the times the crimes were committed, the Prosecution actually does agree with the learned colleagues from the Defence side that there must be a further guidance being provided by the Trial Chamber. To date, both Defence and Prosecution are faced with the problem to not have a very clear guidance what the Trial Chamber actually does understand by using the terms "political, military, and economical context." As the Defence, the Prosecution would appreciate a further clarification and guidance on this issue. Finally, in respect to the general issue of tendering documents into evidence, again the Prosecution is in agreement with the learned colleagues from the Defence side. Taking into account that at the latest by end of March the Prosecution will call its first international witnesses and by end of March this will be the time the Prosecution will tender many, many, many documents -- and the Trial Chamber is well aware of the volume of the documents; namely, about 1.000 documents comprised of more than 3.000 pages -- at that point in time, both parties must be given guidance as to how efficiently they should do it. The Prosecution is much in favour of the approach that has been taken and has been used in the Simic case; however, not only in the Simic case but also earlier on in the Keraterm case, meaning that each party tenders its documents into evidence from the bar table. In practical terms, since Defence already has the exhibit list and knows about the documents the Prosecution intends to tender into evidence since more than four months. Meanwhile I would suggest the Defence should be given a deadline, and it should be a pretty short deadline, to indicate which of these documents they wish to make objections; otherwise, the Prosecution should be allowed to tender such documents into evidence. Of course, the issue of authenticity should not be mixed up with the issue of the admissibility of documents. Again, the Prosecution wishes to emphasise that both parties are in agreement that further guidance of the Trial Chamber must be given in respect to the military and political and economical context, and in particular, in relation to the issue of tendering documents. I also wish to use this opportunity to inform the Trial Chamber, both the Trial Chamber and Defence, that the Prosecution is making efforts to translate all - all - of its documents into the French language and such efforts are being made with the aim to have the documents ready by end of March, beginning of April. "Ready" means translated into the French language. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to confirm that when I mentioned the procedure used in the Tadic and Simic case, as well as in the Blaskic case, it wasn't to make any suggestions to the Trial Chamber. It was only to remind everyone of the various procedures that were followed in various cases. With regard to the Defence's position, we would prefer to proceed in this manner: To tender documents into evidence through the witness. In our opinion, that would make it easier for the Trial Chamber to determine the probative value and the relevance of the document. If we could reach an agreement with the Prosecution with regard to tendering certain documents into evidence, we agree with the Trial Chamber that this procedure could make tendering documents into evidence easier in this case. And one last comment: On last Friday the Defence met with the Prosecution. We wanted to ask about our request for a consolidated list of documents. This would facilitate our task. My learned colleague has now said that the list is already ready. We are waiting for this list, which would make our work a lot easier. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber will naturally deliberate about the points you have mentioned, but it would first of all be good to have a consolidated list of all the documents. That is the first thing that has to be done. And then everyone will see matters more clearly. This work is being done, and let's hope that the Prosecution will be able to have this list ready as soon as possible. In our decision that concerns the expert witness, General Reinhardt, we'll be providing very useful additional information. And naturally, in our decision - and I'm quoting from what I can remember - we have asked the Prosecution to inform us in advance of the issues that are going to be addressed in the course of the examination and also to provide us at the same time with the list of exhibits -- with the list of documents that will be tendered into evidence in the course of the examination of General Reinhardt. This is what we said in our decision. This decision dealt with the questions that you have mentioned, the issues you have mentioned. This procedure might be efficient, and I think that this is the procedure that the Defence would like to follow. But to save time, it would be good to have a list of the documents in advance. I have also pointed out that among the documents there are documents that are important for everyone. There are documents in which units are founded. And in particular, all the documents that relate to General Reinhardt and that he has mentioned in his written report, which has to be modified in accordance with our instructions. Naturally, the Defence already has these documents, and when the expert witness commences his testimony it is at that point in time that the Prosecution will be able to say, "Well, I'm tendering document number 1 into evidence." If the Defence has no objections to document number 1, at that stage we will give it an exhibit number immediately. On the other hand, if the Defence raises an objection, we'll see how to deal with the matter as we proceed, because the procedure is that first of all the witness has to authenticate the document. We have already seen that some documents aren't recognised; they are officially contested. And we saw that in the case of the previous witness who did not contest the contents of an order but he pointed out that the order hadn't been drafted by himself. So you can see the sort of difficulties that we face. We may have documents that are supposed to be issued by a certain person and then the witness might say, "No, in fact, I didn't draw up the document." So we need to have a debate at such a point about the document in question. But if the witness says, "I recognise document number 1," in that case there's no problem; we'll move on to document number 2. So this would allow us to proceed very rapidly. It seems that there are also other questions. We will clarify these matters, questions that have to do with military and political issues. So a document that concerns military logistics, appointments, the functioning of a unit, orders issued by superiors to -- the superiors to subordinates, these are naturally military documents. Such documents have nothing to do with economics or finance. As far as political matters are concerned, these are documents that deal with decisions of a political decision [as interpreted], either at the level of a state or at the level of a community, or at the municipal level. These are documents of political nature. Sometimes the economic sphere and the political sphere can overlap but a document which relates to the HVO -- for example, we saw the document coming from the place called Grude that concerned the HVO. That was a political document, naturally. And you have also noted that there are witnesses who make a distinction between the military and the political sphere. The previous witness said, "I'm a soldier. I have nothing to do with politics." So if you show a military person a political document, the response will be military. So as far as the military documents are concerned, it won't be difficult to categorise these documents. As far as other documents are concerned, economical documents, those that have to do with supplies, transport, circulation, and so on, these are documents that have to do with social matters, financial matters, economical matters. So it's for the parties to make a distinction. So the Trial Chamber can't say, "This document is being categorised as an economical or political or military document." It is for you to say what your position is, and then the Trial Chamber will decide what the relevance, the nature of the document, is what its probative value is. But all this will be based on a debate in the presence of the examination of a witness. We've delayed the parties to proceed. So far we haven't had any difficulties with regard to the documents. You've expressed your fear with regard to the witnesses who will be appearing in the future. We understand your difficulty. But as we are aware of your professionalism, we are sure that the difficulties will be minimal. We need this consolidated list to proceed. And with regard to our decision that concerns General Reinhardt, we also need the list of exhibits and order of the questions that will be put to the witness, and this will enable us to proceed more and more rapidly, I think. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, very briefly. The consolidated list is almost ready to be filed, and the Prosecution will certainly file it in the course of this week. In respect to the documents related to the expert opinion of General Reinhardt, the Prosecution will certainly in the near future file a written submission outlining the different issues that have been addressed by the Trial Chamber in its decision. However, I already wish to use this opportunity now to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to two main issues that will make it quite difficult for the Prosecution to in all aspects comply with the wishes of the Trial Chamber. The military expert General Reinhardt repeatedly - repeatedly in his written statement - has emphasised that he based his opinion on the entirety of documents he has been provided with. Therefore, the Prosecution, which intends to keep the examination-in-chief of General Reinhardt very brief, will have to rely on all documents which have been provided -- which General Reinhardt has been provided with. The issue will become even more complicated in respect to the documents the Prosecution may or may not use during the re-examination of General Reinhardt, since the Prosecution, of course, doesn't know until the end of the cross-examination of General Reinhardt by Defence which documents Defence will use. And the re-examination, of course, depends on the documents used by our learned colleagues during the cross-examination. However, I wish to emphasise that we will elaborate on the related issues in a written submission, which will be filed in near future. Finally, just making reference to a remark in the transcript. The Prosecution noted in the past that quite often legal debates on the admissibility of documents were made in the presence of the witnesses. It appears, at least sometimes, it appears to be advisable to not have the witness present during such debates, since the witness may come to certain conclusions which are not necessarily -- or may not necessarily be the right ones. However, Mr. President, Your Honours, this is a suggestion only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Withopf, the Trial Chamber thanks you for what you have just said. We note that with regard to General Reinhardt it is your intention when conducting an examination-in-chief -- in fact, there are very few questions. You will be relying exclusively on the written statement and you will allow the Defence to conduct its cross-examination. This written statement, naturally, is supported by all the documents that you will inform us of, and you will provide us with a list of these documents. This is a procedure that could be very useful and could enable us to save time. If the Defence has no objections to make, the written report will then be a document you will be tendering into evidence, because this report refers to a number of documents and we'll have the documents, and then the cross-examination can address all the issues raised. This will enable us to save time. You have also mentioned the matter of documents contested and also discussions on admissibility in the presence of witnesses. It's true that it might be good to ask the witness to leave the courtroom, but bear in mind the fact that, as in the case of the previous witness, there were ten documents and objections were made to each one. If on each occasion we ask the witness to leave whenever a document arises to which one objects, this will double the time we spend on the proceedings at least. In addition, a witness following a debate that has to do with the admissibility of evidence might draw certain conclusions from that; that's true. But, on the other hand, asking the witness to leave the courtroom might waste a lot of time. So we have to deal with this on a case-by-case basis. In some cases we'll have to ask the witness to leave, and then naturally there will be other cases in which this won't be necessary in the light of the witness's personality. So we will assess this on a case-by-case basis, and we'll take into consideration the need of not wasting time. As there is no jury - we have professional Judges, a professional Defence team, a professional Prosecution team - we will assess the problems as we proceed and we will find solutions to the problems almost immediately. But we've taken note of the issues raised. You also mentioned another problem, and that has to do with the translation of documents. We would like to thank you for your attempts to have the relevant documents translated, and quite by chance we discovered that a document had already been translated into French, since it was a document that appeared in another case. So perhaps among the documents that you will be using some have already been translated. And in this case, we could avoid translating the same document twice. Our concern, with regard to the translation of documents, is that we don't want documents that have been translated into English translated into French; in the case of important documents, we want B/C/S documents to be translated into French translated into English [as interpreted], so that we can check in the three languages the important of the document. Because if there is a translation from B/C/S into French and B/C/S into English, that's not enough. We need a translation B/C/S-into-English and B/C/S-into-French, and then everyone will be able to assess the situation. I don't know if this is possible, but on a number of occasions we have already seen that there are certain ambiguities as far as the translations are concerned. And if we had two translations, this would enable us to reduce the possibility of errors occurring. So I am turning to the parties. If it is your intention to present documents translated into French, have them translated from B/C/S into French. Don't have them translated from English into French. That's not necessary. We have some knowledge of English, and the adversarial proceedings are such that if we have a text in B/C/S or French or English we'll be able to ask the witness some questions to solve any difficulties that may arise. But in order to reduce any uncertainties, as far as the importance and scope of a document is concerned, I think it would be good if documents in B/C/S were directly translated into French or translated into English, and then we could compare the two translations. But according to the procedure of this Tribunal, the French translation section apparently only translates documents from English. I don't understand why we haven't employed translators who can translate from B/C/S into French or B/C/S into English, but unfortunately this is a problem that may arise. If the Defence can also translate B/C/S documents into English, given the resources it has, so much more the better. And if it can do it into English too, that would be very good. And it would be ideal for everyone if we had the two versions. But if we can only have documents translated from B/C/S into English, then naturally we will work on the basis of these documents. It's now 5.20. We have perhaps another 15 or 20 minutes for the second witness. Are there any special measures that are being required? If that is the case, it is necessary for us to go into private session. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, yes, the Prosecution will in respect to the next witness apply for protective measures. And if we could, please, go into private session for that purpose. My colleague Mr. Stamp will make the oral application for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm giving the floor to the Prosecution for their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, I will be calling you ZC, Mr. ZC. That is your pseudonym during your testimony. So, Witness ZC, were you a member of the HVO in the early part of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And were you captured at some time that year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Immediately before you were captured, where was your unit deployed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main body of my unit was in the Kalin Hotel in Bugojno. And at the moment when I was captured, I was in the Croatian centre; that is, some 20 to 30 metres away from the Kalin Hotel, by the command of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who captured you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: By whom were you captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall the date of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, after your capture, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to the school, to the grammar school. To the basement of that grammar school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The place that you were taken to, was it known by any name in particular? I heard you say -- well, let the question remain as it is. The place that you were taken to, was it known by any name in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you just say that you were taken to the Gimnazija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the grammar school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, prior to your being taken there, do you know what the Gimnazija was used for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean before the war or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, immediately before you were taken there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the base of the military police of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How did you -- well, before -- you said the base. The base of which unit? Or which level of the BiH army was it the headquarters of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were soldiers there belonging to the military police. I believe that the headquarters of the military police was also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was this the headquarters for the military police in all of the municipalities or in Bugojno or at a lower level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the entire municipality of Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, how did you come by this knowledge that it was the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was also a military policeman. I was in the HVO. And we manned checkpoints at the entrance to the town of Bugojno together with the BiH army. So we patrolled together. And this is where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this was before there were conflicts or hostilities began between the ABiH and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, earlier you told us you were taken to the basement of the Gimnazija. When you were taken there, were other prisoners there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were already prisoners there. They belonged to my unit of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how many other prisoners were there in the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 30 and 40, according to my estimate. I believe that that was the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And were you taken there alone or were there other prisoners or detainees taken there at the time that you were taken there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not alone. All those who were put in my cell, some ten of us, we were transferred there. And some others who were in the sports hall of the Gimnazija, those were members of the 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the layout of the basement in relation to the part that you were taken to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ceiling was low. We couldn't stand up straight. Some 40 of us were accommodated there. We were like sardines in a can. We couldn't stretch our legs. The room was narrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you estimate the size of the room, the dimensions of the room, length and width?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was 3 to 4 metres wide and some 10 metres long -- or not even that long, between 8 and 10 metres long. It was dark. There was no light whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, were you able to recognise and identify some of your fellow detainees down there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were already some detainees there when I came. I recognised those sitting close to me or the voices of people that I heard talking. That was the only way I could recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For about how long did you remain at the Gimnazija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some 15 to 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that was from the date you were captured, which you said was the 19th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there until the beginning of August, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to clarify that. That is from the date that you were captured, which is from the 19th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, during that period of time while you were there, can you just describe to the Court the conditions in respect to the diet that you received from your captors.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the first five or six days, we didn't receive anything. I lived on water. We would be given three or four loaves of bread to share between 30 or 40 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect -- you said for the first five or six days you didn't receive anything. Can I take it that you would receive three to four loaves of bread sometime after those first five or six days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the first five or six days, we received those three to four loaves of bread. But there were 30 or 40 of us, so each of us would receive just a tiny little slice a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And after those first few days, did the condition improve or did it remain the same for the duration of your stay there? And we're talking about food for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were somewhat better, but I would say that this was a bare minimum, just to survive. We could not eat as much as we would have wanted to. We didn't receive as much as we would have wanted to. We would receive something in the morning and sometime in the afternoon. Twice a day we would receive some sort of a meal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what was the situation in relation to water for drinking purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended on the guard. There was one who would bring us a bottle of water, so the situation with water was somewhat better. Some knew this guard, and sometimes this guard would bring us water.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what was the situation when this guard was not present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This guard was mostly there, so he did bring us water.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what toilet facilities were there at your disposal, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, it depended on the guards. Some would allow us to go out to the toilet. Or we would use a bucket that we had in the cell and we used the bucket to relieve ourselves in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, while you were there, did they -- how did the guards treat the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two were taken out, Ivkovic and Subasic. They were taken most of the times and they were beaten. And once I saw that this guy Subasic, he was badly beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were Ivkovic and Subasic the only ones beaten while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was someone called Goran. I can't remember his surname. I think he was from Mostar. I think he was born there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how many of the prisoners were beaten -- were taken out and beaten while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Gimnazija, in the grammar school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that this is a leading question. The witness - line 14, page 77 - said that Ivkovic and Subasic were beaten. And then in response to another question put to him as to whether anyone else had been beaten, the witness said that they called out someone called Goran and that he thought he was from Mostar. Now the Prosecution is asking how many other detainees they beat, and this is not something that can be concluded from the previous answers provided by the witness, because the witness's answers were precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I mean, it might very well be a matter of interpretation, but Counsel for the Defence has completely misquoted the two questions I asked, having regard to the official record. And, clearly, the questions are not leading, if one goes by the official record. But it might be a matter of translation. The first question is: Were they the only ones beaten? And the next question -- not the next succeeding question, but a later question was simply: How many prisoners were beaten? Now, I respectfully submit that the -- if the witness has testified that some prisoners were beaten, then it could in no circumstance be a leading question to ask how many in all were beaten. But I think it's really a matter of translation, because I'm quite sure my friend wouldn't misquote what has been said. But on the English transcript, the questions are not leading. In which case, may I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the Gimnazija, how many prisoners in all did you know were beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can remember those three men the most. At the time, they didn't beat me in the grammar school, so I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I do remember these three persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, how did you become aware that these three persons were beaten at the Gimnazija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when they returned, they'd tell us about it or you could see traces of the beatings on them when they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said you remained there until the first week of August 1993. What happened then? Were you taken somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They transferred us from the basement in the grammar school to the school, to the hall in that school. There were other detainees there. We spent one night there. In the morning -- or rather, on the following day, they transferred us in refrigerated lorries to the furniture salon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where was this furniture salon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about 4 or 5 hundred metres from the grammar school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you taken to any particular place in that salon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were also taken to the basement of the furniture salon, where it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Had you been to the furniture salon before that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not inside, not in the furniture salon. But I had passed by.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you describe the basement that you were put in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was a bigger room -- it was a big room. There was some water on the floor, maybe from the sewer system. I don't know where it came from, but there was a lot of water. There was some old furniture or something like that. And we slept on that old furniture or on planks, on wooden planks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long did you remain at the furniture salon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For about 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were there, what were the toilet facilities like that were made available to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was one toilet upstairs, but it was blocked, so it wasn't really possible to use it. It was always blocked. It was very often blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many prisoners were with you in the basement of the furniture salon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but I think that there were about 100 of them. All my colleagues from the military police were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, may we just very briefly go into private session while I ask him a couple of matters of personal detail?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, Witness, without identifying or calling the names of who told you, did they tell you about the beating of any particular prisoner and by whom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, could you make an order to have this answer redacted. Do continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that he had been taken to see Dautovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who, to your knowledge, was this Dautovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the commander of the BH army military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the question I just asked you earlier is: By whom were you told he was beaten? And your answer was: "He was taken to see Dautovic." Just focus on the question that I asked. By whom were you told he was beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And did he tell you who did the beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that he had seen Dautovic and that Dautovic beat him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I got there, I went to see my commander, to greet him. He was lying down. He couldn't move.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Why couldn't he move?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I suppose he had been beaten, because when I appeared, he remained lying down, or when we greeted each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, while you were there, how did the guard treat the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When night fell, they would start calling out the names of people. They would take them out and they would beat them. Sometimes they'd do this to the same persons and sometimes to other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were there, about how many people in all were called out and beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, but quite a lot of people. On one night, perhaps five to six persons. It depended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you observe any particular pattern in relation to who was called out, or did it appear to be at random?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how they decided about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. But how did it appear to you? Did you notice any pattern, or did it appear to be at random?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps at random. I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, tell us, before we move on to you: When persons were called out to be beaten and when they returned, did you notice anything about them? What condition were they in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had bruises on their backs. When they came down, other detainees would help them. They'd put some sort of wet cloths on them, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about yourself, your personal experience? How did the guards treat you while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They also took me out at night, I don't know, about 9.00 or 10.00. But they didn't touch me on that occasion. They sent me back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That occasion was about how long after you had been brought there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, about five or six days after I'd been brought there, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I take it that there was a next occasion, or at least one other occasion. Could you tell us what happened on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. It was on the same night I returned. I wanted to go to sleep, and around midnight I was woken by the other detainees who told me that they were calling me. I went up. There were four or five of them standing there. It was dark. The lights weren't on. Occasionally someone would use a lighter to spread a bit of light. I sat down on a chair, and then they started beating me. They started hitting me. One of them hit me with a truncheon, and the others would punch me or hit me with whatever they could get their hands on. They beat me like that for five or six minutes. I don't know for how long exactly. And then they sent me back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. President, if this time is convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 7.00. We have to adjourn now. Witness, you'll be back for the hearing that will start at 2.15. You should come a little earlier so that the relevant services can take charge of you. During the interim period, you are not to see anyone and you are not to have any contact with representatives from the Prosecution. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's been done. I'll address the Prosecution now. We will have concluded with this witness's testimony tomorrow. And I assume there will be another witness after this one tomorrow. Mr. Withopf, can you provide us with any information?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can we please go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 24th day of February, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 p.m.,
